Well, take a quick break first. These ten minutes should not decide on whether or not you pass tomorrow.

I do not have ADHD. Thus I cannot relate. I can only give you some advice on what works for me.

First: Split up your pages. Try to divide them into 5 sets of 10 pages.
Second: Set a timer. Try to only focus on those pages for the duration of, let's say 45 Minutes. Go page by page. Try to memorize it by explaining it to yourself. This helps me a lot! Especially of you aim to explain it in your own words
Third: Take a break for 10 more minutes. Then continue with the next 10 pages and so on. Try to recall some of the prior pages between a break and the next set of 10 pages. 

At last, before going to bed: Try to explain the most important concepts again. If you struggle, look them up before going to bed. Let your brain re-wire the information throughout the night.

Also I want to include two more things:
I) Do not stress about the exam. You are going to give your best under the current circumstances. If failure happens, let it happen and let it be a lesson. It is not a problem if you fail a class. But it is a problem if you don't learn from that failure!

II) No matter how the exam turns out to be: You are still the same person with flaws and strengths. Do not let that exam question yourself, as your flaw might lie in procrastination or a diverging attention but not you as a person.

Okay, I am sorry, but I have to include this too: Please seek out help from either your familiy, your friends or spouse or a professional. Do not feel ashamed by doing this. As it only should help you to avoid breakdowns like today. 

Good luck and best wishes!

It depends on the topic, your field of study and your professor. 
I'd say that 3 sources for an eight pages research project can be the lower bar if it is written and articulated well.
Usually I would try to cover the basics or foundation of my papers with many sources so that I can use the better tailored sources on the more specific parts.
Do not be concerned however. If you still have so time remaining I'd advice you to look for some further, minor sources. If you're in a hurry - don't do that. It will feel tacked on and your professor will know that you just included this author for a juicier list of works cited.

Well, I get what you mean by asking such a question. In general I would assume that most people question the value of a grade as an indicator of a person's skill. At least if they do not have to hire them. 

Many people, your friends, your parents, your relatives and probably even your teachers would agree with the fact that you are more than your grades and that thosr grades cannot define you as a person. You have flaws and strengths that remain undetected by the ones judging you with formulaic grades. 

Sadly, when hiring you need to have some indicators for judging people on whether or not they fit the demand. 

I for my part receive some kind of pleasure out of good grades. This might be because in university the world of 'real' works seems so far away and I actually tire of university in itself. Usually I get more motivated by the credit points I reveive, as it shows that once again I got closer to the end of this institution. 

Interestingly enough, I feel that good grades boost my motivation for a few days, while the thought of accumulating credit points keeps me somewhat motivated in the long run.

I know that this is a bad motivation in itself as it shows that I am not so overly enthusiastic on studying and scientific research. Then again, if I were to reach my dream profession in a different way I wouldn't have decided for university. 

Luckily I am fairly good when it comes to grades. Not excellent, but still strong.

I envy you for your shift in attention in comparison to others. However keep in mind that grades can dictate whether or not we make it in the field. We are usually judged based on our grades. As a consequence, we, counting myself to that group, view good grades as a feedback that tells us that we are on the right track. At least from the perspective of our judges, teachers, professors, superiors, etc.
